Definition: AI models (like deep neural networks) that function as a black box, handling massive complexity but unable to explain how they reached a conclusion.
Explainable AI -- models designed for transparency and auditability (like decision trees) whose decision-making humans can follow.
Synthetic media generated by AI (using GANs, diffusion models, or voice-cloning systems) to realistically impersonate a human being.
Generative Adversarial Network -- two competing AI networks, a Generator creating fakes and a Discriminator detecting them. One of several techniques used to create realistic synthetic media.

A defense against deepfakes in which media is cryptographically signed (by cameras, editing tools, or AI generators) with a record of its origin and edits, so tampering is detectable. Missing credentials do not prove media is fake.
Using AI (like an LLM) to analyze source code and generate highly targeted inputs to discover vulnerabilities, rather than random mutation.

Malware that changes its outward appearance (and, in its metamorphic form, its code) with each infection. AI makes this cheaper by generating new variants on the fly, evading signature-based antivirus detection.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation -- connecting an LLM to a vector database of proprietary documents so it can answer questions from internal data.
An attack where the user crafts chatbot inputs designed to override the AI's ethical safeguards or system instructions.
An attack that hides a malicious payload in a document later ingested by a RAG system, compromising the AI without direct interaction.
This book's label for a defense-in-depth strategy (privilege separation, a screening second LLM, structured prompting) that protects the trust boundaries around an LLM.
An OWASP LLM vulnerability (renamed Improper Output Handling in 2025) where a downstream system blindly trusts and executes an LLM's output, enabling attacks like XSS or SSRF.
An energy-latency attack that submits resource-intensive prompts (sponge examples) to exhaust GPU resources and spike cloud costs. OWASP now files this under Unbounded Consumption.
An attack during the training phase where an adversary subtly alters the training dataset to insert permanent backdoors into the model.
An attack that probes a model to reconstruct or regurgitate the sensitive data (PII or PHI) it was trained on.
A technique that adds statistical noise to training data or the training process so no single individual's record noticeably affects the model, limiting what model inversion can reveal.
Training a model locally on edge devices and sharing only updated weights, so raw data never leaves the device.
A sanctioned corporate-tier AI environment where the vendor contractually commits that prompts are protected and not used to train public models.
Stealing a trained model, either by exfiltrating its weights or by querying its API at scale to build a copy.
Risks from third-party models, datasets, plug-ins, and libraries, such as backdoored models or unsafe model file formats.
Trusting AI output without verification because it sounds fluent and confident (the illusion of competence).
Giving an AI system more permissions, tools, or autonomy than its task requires, so one bad output or injected instruction can cause real damage.
Plug-ins or tools that give an AI broad permissions or accept unvalidated model output as input.
Technical and policy controls that limit what an AI assistant can accept, say, and do.
